newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany set for next stage of tax battle.
newsitem.headline: Germany set for next stage of tax battle.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Sunday braced themselves for the next stage of a furious battle over tax reform plans.

Two bills on tax cuts for 1998 and 1999 easily passed in the lower house, or Bundestag, where the majority of deputies are from Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP), but were blocked by the opposition-controlled upper huse.
Parliament's mediation committee, made up of 32 members equally divided between the upper and lower houses, meets on Monday to try to thrash out a deal between the two sides.
A day before the committee was set to begin the task of trying to build a bridge the deep differences, leading coalition and opposition members showed few signs they were willing to compromise.

"We are waiting for a signal that makes clear whether the SPD is playing for time -- at the expense of the unemployed -- or whether the SPD-led states in the Bundesrat are willing to move towards reform," FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told the weekly Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
The government bills seek to cut income taxes by a net 30 billion marks ($17 billion) over two years, sharply lower income tax rates, close tax loopholes and change corporate tax rules.

The SPD, which controls a majority of states and therefore has the upper hand in the Bundesrat, rejects the government's idea of cutting the top income tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent and wants instead to lower unit wage costs.
It says so-called supplementary wage costs, extra charges on labour that are not associated with production, should be reduced or removed from unit wages and instead be financed elsewhere.
It has called the government's bills socially unjust and is trying to divide the coalition proposals, hinting it could agree on certain parts but not on the coalition's broad reform.
Gerhardt, however, said the coalition would insist on maintaining the basic direction of the reform, including a net tax cut across the board, or there was little hope of a deal with the SPD.
"The Social Democrats must finally prove they can do more than obstruct," he said. "We can reach an agreement on lower labour costs in Germany."

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine was quoted in Welt am Sonntag as saying the party had no intention of agreeing to the government plans for huge tax cuts that might or might not be fully implemented after general elections in 1998.
"We are not going along with this tax deception," he said.

Meanwhile, the ongoing tax debate was nearly overshadowed at the weekend by Finance Minister Theo Waigel's acknowledgement that the federal budget deficit would surge to 70 billion marks this year from previous forecasts of 53.3 billion.

Despite the ballooning deficit, which threatens German qualification for European monetary union, FDP leader Gerhardt said the coalition would agree on Friday to raise the deficit rather than hike taxes.
"Whoever increases the tax burden in Germany turns up the pressure on the labour market," he said, referring to Germany's more than four million unemployed.
